subject: research/robofab-cell-fesc
professional: a queueing-network / manufacturing-systems performance analyst (the kind who builds flexible-manufacturing-system and automated-cell throughput models) who would first check the reference chain against an independent simulation and then ask which non-product-form decomposition literature the result is positioned against

evidence.correctness: Recomputed independently, using a discrete-event simulation I wrote from the cell description (not reusing ctmc.py): (1) N=1 closed form, cycle = 2+20+2+3 = 27 min, good rate = 60*0.85/27 = 1.8889/h; ctmc.throughput(1,1,1,20,2,2,3,.15) gives 1.88889, simulation 1.886. (2) Exact chain vs 3e6-minute simulation: P=2,N=4,k=1 exact 4.125 vs sim 4.126; P=4,N=6,k=4 exact 7.554 vs sim 7.557; P=2,N=2 exact 3.653 vs sim 3.649/3.649/3.653 (three seeds). (3) The decomposition's claimed negative bias is real, not an artefact of the reference: P=6,N=8,k=1 fesc is 1.40% under the exact 9.949 and the independent simulation gives 9.96. The reference the whole study rests on is therefore sound. Also ran the 5 tests (pass) and spot-checked results.txt rows against the code; I did not re-run experiments/run.py because it overwrites tracked result files.
evidence.completeness: Claims checked: 42 settings table present in results.txt (42 rows counted) with the stated MAE 0.32/max 1.57 for fesc, 6.77/20.29 plain, 4.34/12.20 held; 4 over/38 under; 5 larger cells up to 17,919 states (P=8,N=16,k=4); figure error.png, paper/whitepaper.md, refs.bib all exist; 5 tests claimed and 5 found; ctmc.py and mva.py claimed copied unchanged and diff against research/robofab-cell-ctmc confirms identical. Project is listed in research/README.md. Everything stated as done is present. Minor: ctmc.py docstring points at a sim.py that is not in this project; refs.bib contains an unused Little 1961 entry.
evidence.verification: PYTHONPATH=src python3 -m unittest discover -s tests: 5 tests OK; pytest 5 passed. Mutation 1 in fesc.py fesc_rate: changed the birth-death up-rate index H[N-m] to H[N-m-1] (an off-by-one that makes the decomposition wrong): ALL 5 TESTS STILL PASSED (survived). Reason: the closeness tests use loose tolerances (2% for one printer, only 'beats plain MVA' for N=8,P=4) and the exact-equality test uses N=1 where the birth-death chain has two states. Mutation 2 (disable unload priority in the subsystem dispatch): 5 of 5 tests failed (caught, though non-specifically). Both reverted with git checkout; git status clean. The 42-row accuracy table is the real test, but nothing in tests/ pins it, so a regression in the core aggregation step would not fail CI. No test checks the exact chain itself against an independent solution (hand case, known product-form limit or simulation).
evidence.craft: Read ctmc.py, fesc.py, mva.py, run.py, figure.py, test_fesc.py. Defects: fesc.py duplicates _dispatch and the whole transition-generation loop of ctmc.build (about 40 lines) with the inspection state removed, instead of parameterising build; subsystem_rate has an unused is_unload parameter in add(); ctmc.py and mva.py are copied wholesale from a sibling project rather than imported (mva.py ships unused cell_demands/balanced_bounds branches); stationary() power iteration returns silently on max_iter without a convergence warning and np.add.at is slow; run.py group selector for 'N = 2P' relies on an operator-precedence-dependent and/or expression; results are only valid for hard-coded exponential load/unload/inspect with no input validation. Code is short, deterministic and readable, but a reviewer would ask for the duplication to go.
evidence.claims: README headline numbers all match results.txt (0.32%, 1.57%, 6.8%, 20.3%, 4.3%, 12.2%, 38/42, 17,919 states, 1,749 sub-states). Honest limits stated: stylised, 42 settings only, error 'may be larger elsewhere', no explanation of the sign, no speed claim (and results.txt confirms exact 0.8 s vs decomposition 0.8 s so none is supportable). The README records its own failed exactness test. Weaknesses: the title says 'without enumerating its states' but the method enumerates a smaller Markov chain at each population, i.e. it still enumerates states; the headline '0.3%' is for the author's chosen inspector speed (3 min), and the sibling project research/robofab-cell-fescsweep (listed in research/README.md) later found the error peaks at -2% to -5% when the inspector speed varies, ten times the headline; this README only hints at it in 'Next steps'. Bibliography is flagged as not re-checked online. Disclaimer 'stylised, simulation-only, no physical cell' present.
evidence.fitness: A researcher can build on it: the code runs in about 3 s, is deterministic, and the sibling fescsweep project did build on it. But novelty is thin. Flow-equivalent-server / Norton aggregation of closed networks with load-dependent servers is textbook (Chandy-Herzog-Woo 1975, Bolch et al.), and its application to automated cells and FMS with blocking and non-product-form behaviour, with known corrections (Marie's method, Baynat-Dallery, Buzacott-Shanthikumar FMS models), is long established. The paper cites only Reiser-Lavenberg, Bolch, Chandy and an unused Little entry, and no non-product-form decomposition or FMS literature, and no prior work comparing against exact chains for robotic cells. The result (a good approximation on 42 hand-picked settings of one illustrative cell with made-up step times) is a sound but small replication-level finding, not a publishable result by itself; no real cell data. A practitioner could not use it to size a real cell.
evidence.domain: A senior performance analyst would accept the method (short-circuit the subsystem, tabulate H(n), solve the birth-death chain) as the standard Norton construction and would accept the comparison against the exact chain as the right test. They would object that (a) the exactness argument is wrong for this system class and the literature on non-product-form aggregation (blocking-after-service, simultaneous resource possession, unload priority) is not engaged; (b) the inspection station is exponential and the only variability varied is print-phase Erlang order, so robustness to inspection/arm variability is untested; (c) validation is against a Markov model with the same exponential assumptions, not against a general-distribution simulation or a real cell, so 'error against the exact chain' measures the approximation, not the prediction error of a physical cell; (d) the directional bias is unexplained; (e) the parameter set (2/2/3 min, 15% fail) is illustrative, not sourced from any printer/arm datasheet, contrary to research/CLAUDE.md's 'run the numbers' guidance.

defects.what: Surviving mutation: an off-by-one in the birth-death up-rate (H[N-m] to H[N-m-1]) in fesc_rate passes all 5 tests; no test pins the aggregation step or the 42-row accuracy table

Headline 0.3% mean error is for one inspector speed; the sibling fescsweep project found -2% to -5% peaks when the inspector speed varies, and this README/paper do not say so in the claims or limitations beyond a 'Next steps' mention
Novelty and prior work: Norton/FES aggregation of FMS and automated cells with non-product-form corrections is long established; paper cites none of that literature and positions the result as new

Title/README say 'without enumerating its states' though the method solves a Markov chain on up to 1,749 states per population; saving is only a state-count ratio with no timing benefit (0.8 s vs 0.8 s)

fesc.py copies ctmc.build's transition loop and _dispatch; unused is_unload argument; ctmc.py and mva.py are copied files; refs.bib has unused Little 1961; ctmc.py docstring references a sim.py not present
stationary() returns silently at max_iter without a convergence check

verdict: A small, honest, correct piece of queueing work: I confirmed the exact reference chain against an independent discrete-event simulation (three settings within 0.1%, plus the N=1 hand value 1.8889/h), confirmed that the decomposition's headline numbers match results.txt and that its small negative bias is genuine, and found no wrong number. It does not meet the bar for three reasons a reader can check: the test suite lets an off-by-one in the core aggregation step through (seeded mutation survived), the novelty is weak because the paper does not engage the established Norton/FMS non-product-form literature and tests one hand-picked illustrative cell with unsourced step times, and the 0.3% headline is for a single inspector speed that the follow-up project later showed can hide errors of 2-5%. Finished (completeness 3) but a replication-level, junior-to-mid result (median 3 of seven dimensions is 2), not a publishable one. Recommended small fix: add a test pinning the 42-row fesc errors (or a few of them, e.g. P=6,N=8,k=1 -1.40% within 0.05) so the surviving mutation fails, and add one sentence to the README limitations citing fescsweep's -2% to -5% peak.
